bridge: Builds on S03 MACs, S04 signatures and S06 session policy. Use only the decoded teaching claims below; no real access token is required.
teaching:
Read the teaching claims as labelled assertions: iss (issuer) says who issued the token; aud (audience) says which service it is intended for; exp (expiry) gives its time deadline. A bearer token grants usable authority to whoever holds it, so avoid copying real tokens into notes. The algorithm is the verification method; RS256 is a standard RSA-signature profile, not encryption of the readable claims. The verifier must already know which issuers, keys and algorithms it trusts. All required checks must pass together.

A JWT compact representation separates encoded header, payload and signature/MAC. Decoding is not verification. Base64url makes bytes representable as text and provides no secrecy or authenticity by itself.

A verifier must use an explicit accepted algorithm/key policy and validate relevant claims such as issuer, audience and expiry. The token's own algorithm label is input, not authority to choose an insecure verifier. Key rotation and key identifiers require a trusted lookup policy; do not fetch arbitrary key material from caller-controlled locations.

A valid token still needs object authorisation and lifecycle decisions. A token may remain cryptographically valid after a user loses a role unless the system checks current state or has a deliberate revocation/expiry design. Keep access and identity tokens' purposes separate and follow the identity provider's exact documentation.
example:
Verifier policy: issuer=https://issuer.example; audience=notes-api;
algorithm=selected RS256 implementation; current time=1000
A: correct signature, iss correct, aud notes-api, exp 1100 -> accept
B: same but aud other-api -> reject
C: same but exp 900       -> reject
D: modified payload with old signature -> reject
E: decoded claims only, no verification -> never treat as authenticated
explanation: All claim values are fictional. The fixture avoids hand-writing a verifier: a maintained JWT library must handle signature encoding and cryptographic validation. Token acceptance is a conjunction of required checks, not a choice of whichever check succeeds.
exercise: Evaluate all five cases and add a correct signature with the wrong issuer and a token requesting an unsupported algorithm. State which policy check rejects each.
solution: Only A is accepted. Wrong audience, expired, modified, unverified, wrong issuer and unsupported algorithm reject for their respective reasons. A valid signature does not waive claim requirements.
challenge: A token for user A is valid for notes-api and unexpired. A requests B's note. Explain both token validation and the separate object decision, including a test that distinguishes them.
challenge_solution: Token validation authenticates A under the policy; ownership still denies B's note. Test A's own note as allowed and B's as denied using the same valid token. Never interpret successful JWT verification as universal data access.
